issues.legal_issue: The statutory requirement to publish an estate-vesting notification in newspapers, as well as in the official gazette, is mandatory when that requirement applies.
material_facts: The notification declared that an estate would vest in the State and thereby affect the proprietor’s vested rights.
The applicable version of the statute required publication in the official gazette and in at least two issues of two newspapers.
issues.conclusion: Publication in the required newspaper issues was mandatory and could not be treated as merely directory.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 3(2) and 4(a) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, the notification had to be published in the manner prescribed by section 3(2) before the vesting consequences under section 4(a) could take effect. The definition of the date of vesting in section 2(h), referring to publication in the Official Gazette, fixed the date from which vesting would operate once the required publication was complete; it did not dispense with the newspaper publications. The Court distinguished Raza Buland Sugar Co. Ltd. v. Municipal Board, Rampur, [1965] 1 S.C.R. 970, and disapproved Rebati Ranjan v. State of Bihar, A.I.R. 1953 Patna 121.

predicates.estate_vesting_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether a notification caused an estate to vest in the State.
predicates.notification_transfers_proprietary_right: The notification would transfer the proprietor’s rights in the estate to the State.
predicates.notification_required_publication_beyond: The applicable legal requirements called for publication of the notification beyond its publication in the official gazette.
predicates.additional_publication_is_mandatory: The required publication beyond the official gazette must be completed before the notification can produce its vesting effect.

issues.definition: When a vesting notification transfers proprietary rights and the applicable requirements call for publication beyond the official gazette, that additional publication is mandatory.

issues.legal_issue: An estate does not vest under a notification when the publication requirements applicable to that notification have not been completed.
material_facts: The notification was published in the Official Gazette but was not shown to have been published in two issues of two newspapers at that time.
The State did not establish that the notification was published in the required newspaper issues later.
The proprietor remained in possession, and the parties proceeded on the basis that he was dispossessed at a later date.
issues.conclusion: The notification did not vest the estate in the State when it was published in the Official Gazette alone; the proprietor was not divested at that stage.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3(2) and 4(a) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, required publication in the full manner specified by section 3(2) before the consequences of vesting under section 4(a) arose. Section 2(h) identified the Gazette publication date as the date from which vesting would take effect once the required publications had been completed. The Court’s interpretation accords with its distinction of Raza Buland Sugar Co. Ltd. v. Municipal Board, Rampur, [1965] 1 S.C.R. 970, and its rejection of the approach in Rebati Ranjan v. State of Bihar, A.I.R. 1953 Patna 121.

predicates.estate_vesting_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether a notification caused an estate to vest in the State.
predicates.notification_published_in_gazette: The notification was published in the official gazette.
predicates.required_newspaper_publication_not_compl: The publication required in newspaper issues was not completed.
predicates.estate_does_not_vest_until_required_publ: The estate remains unvested under the notification until the required publication is completed.

issues.definition: When a vesting notification is published in the official gazette but its required newspaper publication is incomplete, the estate does not vest until that publication is completed.

issues.legal_issue: A later amendment removing a publication requirement does not retrospectively validate earlier notifications that failed to comply with that requirement when the amendment does not operate retrospectively.
material_facts: A later amendment removed the requirement to publish notifications in newspaper issues.
The amendment made certain changes to another subsection retrospectively but did not make the change removing the newspaper-publication requirement retrospective.
The notification at issue had not been shown to satisfy the newspaper-publication requirement applicable when it was issued.
issues.conclusion: The amendment did not retrospectively make the noncompliant notification effective.
issues.legal_principle: The Bihar Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1954 amended section 3(2) to remove the newspaper-publication requirement but did not make that amendment retrospective, although it expressly made specified amendments to section 3(3) retrospective. The Court inferred that the earlier publication requirement remained material to notifications issued before the amendment and that earlier failures to comply were not retrospectively cured.

rule.if: estate_vesting_proceeding and earlier_notification_noncompliant and later_amendment_removed_publication_requirement and amendment_not_made_retroactive

predicates.estate_vesting_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether a notification caused an estate to vest in the State.
predicates.earlier_notification_noncompliant: The notification did not satisfy a publication requirement that applied when it was issued.
predicates.later_amendment_removed_publication_requ: A later amendment removed the publication requirement that had applied to the notification.
predicates.amendment_not_made_retroactive: The amendment did not state that the removal of the publication requirement applied retrospectively.
predicates.earlier_notification_remains_ineffective: The earlier notification is not made effective by the later amendment.

issues.definition: If an earlier notification failed to meet an applicable publication requirement and a later amendment removes that requirement without retrospective effect, the earlier notification remains ineffective.

issues.legal_issue: Lease money for rights exercised while the lessor remained proprietor is payable to the lessor rather than to the State.
material_facts: The proprietor granted a lease while he had not yet been divested of his rights in the estate.
The lessee exercised the leased rights and completed the relevant collection before the State took over the estate.
The State later demanded and received lease money for the same period, which the lessee paid under protest.
issues.conclusion: The lessor was entitled to retain the lease money, and the State was not entitled to collect it for the period in question.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 4(a) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, the State acquired the relevant interests only when the vesting consequences took effect after the required publication. Until then, the proprietor could grant the lease and receive its consideration; the State could not collect lease money for rights already exercised before vesting. The result also followed from the Court’s interpretation of sections 3(2) and 2(h).

predicates.lease_money_recovery_proceeding: The proceeding concerns recovery of lease money claimed by both a lessor and the State.
predicates.lessor_remained_proprietor_when_lease_wa: The lessor still held the proprietary rights when the lease was granted.
predicates.lessee_exercised_lease_before_vesting: The lessee exercised the leased rights before the estate vested in the State.
predicates.state_collected_lease_money_for_that_per: The State collected lease money for the period in which the lessee exercised the lease.
predicates.lease_money_is_payable_to_lessor_not_sta: The lessor, rather than the State, is entitled to the lease money for that period.

issues.definition: When the lessor still holds the proprietary rights at the grant of the lease and the lessee exercises it before vesting, lease money collected for that period belongs to the lessor rather than the State.
